extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and lawyers handling preliminary injunction motions in patent infringement cases
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and substantive criteria that courts apply when deciding motions for preliminary injunctions in patent litigation, including required presumptions (validity, infringement, title), proof standards, acquiescence, prior adjudications, and balancing of harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of security/bond under Clayton Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Clayton Act went into effect, security must be required as a condition of granting either a restraining order or a temporary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously courts could grant such orders with or without security at their discretion; after the Act, a bond (security) is mandatory as a condition of those equitable writs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable injury / danger from delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant must show there appears to be danger of irreparable injury from delay to obtain a preliminary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defendant denies infringement and states he has abandoned infringement and will not further infringe, danger of irreparable injury is not shown. The plaintiff must specifically establish irreparable harm rather than rely on conclusory affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part prima facie foundation (two presumptions and one certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge is guided by two presumptions (patent validity and defendant's infringement) and one certainty (the complainant's title) in deciding if a prima facie case for a preliminary injunction is made out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either presumption or the certainty is absent, no preliminary injunction will be granted except in unusual circumstances; when all are present, injunction will be granted unless defendant interposes some good defense or posts bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources that give rise to a presumption of patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A special presumption of validity exists where the patent has been adjudicated in a Federal court and held valid, where the public has suitably acquiesced in its validity, where a decree pro confesso has been taken, where the defendant does not deny validity, or where the patent succeeded in an interference or contested Patent Office proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption does not arise merely from an unattended letters patent. The text cites many cases showing these distinct factual bases for the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and character of a prior adjudication as foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjudication in another case must result from a regular hearing in equity or trial at law to furnish a suitable foundation for an injunction; interlocutory decrees may be as effective as final decrees for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity adjudications raise a stronger presumption than law trials. Prior adjudication of one claim may support an injunction as to a narrower claim specifying the same invention, but a prior adjudication of an original patent cannot be used to support injunctions for new claims in a reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preclusive force of prior decisions varies by tribunal and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior adjudication of the Supreme Court or Circuit Court of Appeals is conclusive as to the questions it covered; lower court adjudications will be followed unless inconsistent with an equal or higher court decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A jury verdict followed by judgment and refusal to grant a new trial has similar weight to an equity adjudication. Foreign adjudications are not controlling but may be given fair consideration. Prior adjudications based on estoppel, consent, or other non-recognized grounds do not constitute a foundation for injunctions against other defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acquiescence as a foundation for validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acquiescence may create a presumption of validity where patentees made and sold specimens for many years without anyone else attempting to make them, or where patentee long licensed others and no one made or sold without license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiescence from exclusive use of a thing containing several patents does not raise a special presumption in favor of any particular patent claim. When acquiescence stops for good reasons, the presumption ends. Mere manufacture and sale of an alleged patented article does not necessarily constitute acquiescence in the patent that claims it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and quality of acquiescence depends on invention and market
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of time necessary for exclusive possession/acquiescence to support a preliminary injunction depends on the nature of the invention, how naturally it would be used if free to the public, and the popularity with the relevant market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nobody but patentee had use for the article or its merits were so low no one would adopt it, lapse of time doesn't raise a presumption. By contrast, general, genuine acquiescence (e.g., two years with 105,000 specimens sold; eight years with 150 specimens) can be sufficient depending on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses and royalties as evidence of acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficacy of licenses to raise a presumption of acquiescence depends on whether they were issued for substantial royalties or for a nominal price intended merely to raise presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial royalties make licenses as efficacious as sales of specimens; nominal payments require long and genuine royalty payments before licenses have importance in preliminary injunction contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence strengthened by subsequent costly submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence is strengthened when persons who initially refused later, after further information, submit to the patentee's exclusive right—particularly when the submission was costly to the submitter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal acquiescence is not necessary. But where defendant has long possessed and used the invention adversely under claim and color of right, a preliminary injunction will not be granted on basis of acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing of hardships / relative benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when validity and infringement are proven, courts will consider relative benefits to parties and may deny an injunction when injury to defendant would be pronouncedly greater than benefits to plaintiff from the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general equitable proposition governing issuance of preliminary injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decree pro confesso effect limited to that case
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree pro confesso entered in a case raises a sufficient presumption of validity to support a preliminary injunction in that case, but cannot be given the same effect against other defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a decree is limited in its operation to the consenting/defaulting defendant's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent decrees insufficient against third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A consent decree cannot be a proper foundation for a preliminary injunction against third persons unless it appears the defendant consented because his defense had become hopeless (not merely inexpedient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the motive for consent is seldom known, consent decrees are generally useless on motions for preliminary injunctions against anyone other than the consenting defendant or someone in privity with him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission or lack of denial in pleadings raises presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a defendant admits or does not deny validity in his pleadings, such admission or lack of denial raises a sufficient presumption of validity to furnish a foundation for a preliminary injunction in that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between the parties, courts may assume true facts expressly or tacitly admitted by defendant. If validity is disputed only on a ground susceptible of immediate decision, the court may decide it on the motion and grant an injunction if favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited effect of Patent Office interference decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference decision of the Patent Office raises a sufficient presumption of validity to support a preliminary injunction where the defendant is the person (or legal representative/assignee) defeated in the interference and denies validity only on that ground; interference decisions generally cannot be invoked against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interference decision does not have the force of a court adjudication unless the question of priority is the only issue in the suit, though a Court of Appeals decision on an interference may establish a primary case of validity even against third parties. Interference decisions also do not address defenses not involved in the interference (e.g., prior public use or on-sale bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear title to the patent is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant's title to the patent must be clear to obtain a preliminary injunction; the best evidence is the patent if the complainant is patentee, otherwise original assignments or grants must be produced and proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where title papers require judicial construction, the court should construe them on the motion rather than postpone to final hearing unless evidence aliunde is necessary to interpret them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of infringement / danger of infringement must be clear and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant must clearly prove infringement or danger of infringement to obtain a preliminary injunction; danger may be shown by advertising infringing articles or possession of articles the use of which would infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising is conclusive evidence of danger; possession can be counteracted by proof of no intention to use/sell in the country. Infringement cannot be proved by affidavits merely stating the conclusion—plaintiff must prove specific character of defendant's doings. A single sale indicating readiness to make further sales may suffice to show intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show irreparable injury (effect of defendant as mere user)
rubrics_metrics.description: It must appear that irreparable injury to the complainant will result from continued infringement during the suit; that defendant is a mere user tends strongly to negative such irreparable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not generally forego an injunction on the basis of a defendant's simple promise to stop; proof that infringing acts ceased but with a promise to resume is not usually sufficient to avert injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for court's infringement decision on motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Court will examine the infringement question on the motion in light of expert testimony and its construction of the patent; the construction will generally follow that given in the adjudicated case on which presumption of validity is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If infringement depends on a new and enlarged construction of the patent, a preliminary injunction will be denied. If more evidence is needed, court will decline to grant injunction until supplied, though it may require bonds and accounts from defendant in the meantime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's evidentiary defenses: traverse vs confession & avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses to a motion may be by traverse (denying facts) or by confession and avoidance (admitting but alleging new facts); a denial alone is useless unless supported by contradicting affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defendant's affidavits contradict complainant's, the judge will refuse injunction if he believes defendant's affidavits or cannot decide which are true. Because injunctions are summary and potentially dangerous, courts will not apply them where complainant's prima facie evidence is overthrown or seriously damaged by defendant's evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averting the effect of prior adjudication by new defense or other circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a prior adjudication may be averted by proof of some good defence to the patent that was not interposed in the prior adjudicated case, though some courts require such a new defence to be established beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other ways to avert the prior adjudication's effect include showing inconsistency with a former decision, that the adjudicated case is under rehearing, that a jury verdict is pending new trial, that the case has been appealed, or that an unpleaded prior use would have produced a contrary result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope and origination of injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction may be based on infringing acts done before the bill was filed, and successive preliminary injunctions may be obtained to suppress subsequent infringing acts; but if no act was done or threatened before filing, no injunction will be granted under that bill to suppress acts begun after suit commencement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits relief to infringing conduct that either preceded or was reasonably threatened at the time the bill was filed; subsequent wholly new acts begun after filing are not grounds for injunction on the preexisting bill.
